'''Jami Valentine Miller''' (born December 3, 1974) is a patent examiner at the [[United States Patent and Trademark Office]]. She was the first African American woman to graduate with a PhD in physics from [[Johns Hopkins University]]. She created the website AAWIP.com,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://aawip.com/|title=AAWIP|website=aawip.com|access-date=7 September 2018}}</ref> which celebrates African American Women in Physics.

== Early life and education ==
Valentine was born in [[Philadelphia]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Jami Valentine Miller Inspires the Next Generation|url=http://www.aps.org/publications/apsnews/202011/miller.cfm|access-date=2021-08-02|website=www.aps.org|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-02-26|title=Dr. First Jami Valentine Miller|url=https://www.spsnational.org/the-sps-observer/winter/2019/dr-first-jami-valentine-miller|access-date=2021-08-02|website=Society of Physics Students|language=en}}</ref> During junior high she joined the Philadelphia Regional Introduction for Minorities to Engineering (PRIME) program, which prepared her for a career in physics or mathematics.<ref name=":0">{{Cite news|url=https://www.science.org/content/article/defending-your-graduate-life|title=Defending Your Graduate Life|date=2005-09-23|work=Science {{!}} AAAS|access-date=2018-05-01|language=en}}</ref> She attended high school at [[Murrell Dobbins Vocational School]], graduating in 1992.<ref name=":0" /> She completed a bachelor's degree in physics at [[Florida A&M University]], which she graduated [[Latin honors|cum laude]] in 1996.<ref name=":1">{{Cite news|url=http://www.famunews.com/2015/11/alumni-spotlight-qa-with-jami-valentine-ph-d/|title=Alumni Spotlight Q&A with Jami Valentine, Ph.D.|date=2015-11-25|work=FAMU Forward|access-date=2018-05-01|language=en-US}}</ref> Whilst at [[Florida A&M University|FAMU]] she was a "Life-Gets-Better" scholar, which allowed her to work as a summer research assistant at [[Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.drjami.com/ |title=Jami Valentine Miller, PhD |website=drjami.com}}</ref> She also worked in the Center for Nonlinear and Nonequilibrium Aeroscience.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://rattlernation.blogspot.co.uk/2006/05/for-one-new-rattler-phd-life-is-about.html|title=For One New Rattler Ph.D, Life is about to Get Better!|website=rattlernation.blogspot.co.uk|date=3 May 2006|language=en|access-date=2018-05-01}}</ref> Upon graduating from Fame, she moved on to [[Brown University]] for her postgraduate studies, earning a master's degree in 1998.<ref name=":1" /> Valentine studied under [[Chia-Ling Chien]] at [[Johns Hopkins University]], where she worked on [[spintronics]].<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://sites.krieger.jhu.edu/chienlab/people/|title=People {{!}} Nanostructured Materials Lab {{!}} Johns Hopkins University|website=sites.krieger.jhu.edu|date=10 September 2013 |language=en|access-date=2018-05-01}}</ref> Her research focused on novel [[rare earth metal]]s for memory applications.<ref name=":0" /> She successfully defended her dissertation, "Spin Polarization Measurements of Rare Earth Thin Films", in 2006.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.waterstones.com/book/spin-polarization-measurements-of-rare-earth-thin-films/jami-valentine/9783639095135|title=Spin Polarization Measurements of Rare Earth Thin Films by Jami Valentine {{!}} Waterstones|website=www.waterstones.com|language=en|access-date=2018-05-01}}</ref>

== Career ==
As a PhD student, Valentine realized that there were not many professors who looked like her.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://www.brown.edu/academics/physics/news/2017/02/dr-jami-valentine-honored-national-society-black-physicists|title=Dr. Jami Valentine Honored by the National Society of Black Physicists |publisher=Brown University|language=en|access-date=2018-05-01}}</ref> From 1973 to 2012, only 66 black American women earned PhDs in physics, compared to 22,172 white men.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://qz.com/432756/in-39-years-us-physics-doctorates-went-to-66-black-women-and-22000-white-men/|title=In 39 years, US physics doctorates went to 66 black women—and 22,000 white men|last=Kohli|first=Sonali|work=Quartz|access-date=2018-05-01|language=en-US}}</ref> She became involved with national efforts to improve diversity in physics.<ref>{{Cite book|chapter=Women in Physics in the U.S.: A Progress Report|doi=10.1063/1.2128320|title=AIP Conference Proceedings|volume=795|pages=175–178|year=2005|last1=Budil|first1=Kimberly S.}}</ref> She developed the nonprofit African American Women in Physics  [http://aawip.com/ (AAWIP)], which honors the contributions of African American women to physics.<ref name=":2" /> She has made efforts to meet and document as many of them as she can.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.denverpost.com/2007/04/22/scientist-a-pioneer-in-physics/|title=Scientist a pioneer in physics|date=2007-04-22|work=The Denver Post|access-date=2018-05-01|language=en-US}}</ref> She has worked with the [[National Society of Black Physicists]] to increase awareness of underrepresented groups to physics.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://aawip.com/about/|title=About – AAWIP|website=aawip.com|language=en-US|access-date=2018-05-01}}</ref>

Valentine joined the [[United States Patent and Trademark Office]] as an electrical engineer, working on semiconductor and spintronic memory devices.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.nsbp.org/nsbp-news/bhm-physics-profiles/2017-honorees/23-jami-valentine|title=Jami Valentine|last=Roberson|first=Stephen|website=www.nsbp.org|language=en-gb|access-date=2018-05-01}}</ref><ref name=":2" /> In 2012 she was appointed primary examiner.<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.federalpay.org/employees/patent-and-trademark-office/valentine-jami-m|title=Employee Profile of Jami M. Valentine — Patent Examiner|website=www.federalpay.org|language=en|access-date=2018-05-01}}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
Valentine has been an invited speaker at several physics conferences as well as appearing on podcasts.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://advance.osu.edu/webinar-views-from-the-pipeline-women-of-color-in-the-stem-professoriate-427-100pm/|title=Webinar: "Views from the Pipeline: Women of Color in the STEM Professoriate", 4/27, 1:00pm {{!}} Ohio State ADVANCE|website=advance.osu.edu|language=en|access-date=2018-05-01|archive-date=2018-06-26|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180626083047/http://advance.osu.edu/webinar-views-from-the-pipeline-women-of-color-in-the-stem-professoriate-427-100pm/|url-status=dead}}</ref> In February 2017 she was honored by the [[National Society of Black Physicists]] for distinguished service to the organization.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://womeninastronomy.blogspot.co.uk/2017/02/aaswomen-newsletter-for-february-17-2017.html#item3|title=AASWomen Newsletter for February 17, 2017|website=womeninastronomy.blogspot.co.uk|date=17 February 2017|access-date=2018-05-01}}</ref> In 2016, she was honored with the Florida A & M University Distinguished Alumni Award.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Dobson |first1=Byron |title=Local FAMU grads to be honored at FAMUNAA convention |url=https://www.tallahassee.com/story/news/2016/05/26/local-famu-grads-honored-famunaa-convention/84988210/ |work=Tallahassee Democrat |date=May 26, 2016}}</ref> She was an invited plenary speaker for the 2019 Physics Congress where she was to address more than 1,500 physics and astronomy students.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.sigmapisigma.org/sigmapisigma/congress/2019|title=PhysCon 2019 – Making Waves & Breaking Boundaries|date=13 December 2017|access-date=7 September 2018}}</ref> In 2022 she was honored with the Johns Hopkins University Distinguished Alumna Award.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://alumni.jhu.edu/awards/distinguishedalumni | title=The Distinguished Alumnus/A Award &#124; Johns Hopkins Alumni }}</ref>

She was named a [[Fellow of the American Physical Society]] in 2023, "for extraordinary contributions to diversity and inclusion in physics, both in the United States and internationally, and for essential contributions to the history and promotion of Black women in American physics, through the founding of African-American Women in Physics, Inc".<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/fellowships/archive-all.cfm?initial=&year=2023|title=2023 Fellows|work=APS Fellow Archive|publisher=American Physical Society|access-date=2023-10-19}}</ref>

In 2023 she was appointed to the Johns Hopkins University Krieger School of Arts and Sciences Advisory Board. She also sits on the Physics and Astronomy Advisory Council for Hopkins.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://krieger.jhu.edu/giving/alumni/ | title=Alumni }}</ref>
